highlights: Building the next generation of Autodesk's access control system
Created a self-service platform for product teams to define and manage their own permission rules
Rebuilt the onboarding experience — docs and live demos — until new teammates called it the clearest explanation of the platform they'd had

bullets: Building the next generation of Autodesk's access control system — the technology that determines who is allowed to access what within their products. Created a self-service platform that lets product teams define and manage their own permission rules in a structured, consistent way.

Access control is critical infrastructure, and in a microservices company teams are naturally wary of moving something this sensitive onto an unproven system — made harder by the fact that the platform's flexibility, built to model complex permission scenarios, meant a real learning curve before a team saw any payoff. Partnered with a UX engineer to rewrite the documentation from scratch, breaking it into a guided path instead of a full-flexibility dump, and recorded demo walkthroughs of the platform end to end.

Proudest part of this was being able to stand in front of another team, take a real business use case, and demo — step by step, live — how it translates into a working permission rule on the platform. The feedback that mattered most: teammates who'd just joined ACM said the demos were the clearest explanation of the platform they'd gotten, including from people who'd already been on the team a while.
Two teams are currently onboarding in staging, with a production rollout next.
sections.eli5: Think of it like a bouncer checking people into a concert: there's a rule for who's allowed in, a window of time it applies (doors open until the show starts), and a specific thing that gets checked at the door (the barcode on the ticket). Building that bouncer wasn't the hard part — the hard part was teaching every venue how to describe their own "who's allowed in, and when" in those same three pieces, without needing us standing at the door every time.

highlights: 3 years across Payments, Platform, DevSecOps, and Internal App teams
Built the GitHub Actions + Nx CI/CD pipeline powering the whole monorepo for frontend team to deploy frontend applications
Unified subscription/payment systems across multiple VPN brands into one backend system
Automated internal workflows, including full employee onboard/offboarding, creating SCIM connectors

bullets: Designed and built a monorepo platform using Nx and GitHub Actions that let frontend teams ship microfrontend apps and run fast A/B tests. Centralized what used to be a separate deployment pipeline per repo into one shared, standardized setup — including a full CI suite (Playwright end-to-end tests among others) — with typical deploys taking 15-25 minutes.

Nx's dependency graph means a change only rebuilds, tests, and deploys the specific apps and libraries it actually affects, rather than the whole monorepo. Wiring this into CI wasn't turnkey at the time — no official tooling existed yet — so wrote a custom script to compute the affected project list inside GitHub Actions; Nx later shipped an official action solving the same problem.

The bigger win was speed to start, not just speed to ship: launching a brand-new frontend app used to mean creating a new GitHub repo, copying and hand-editing a CI/CD pipeline, and writing new infrastructure-as-code from scratch — real work before a single line of the actual app existed. Built a generator that scaffolds a fully wired app — pipeline and infrastructure included — in one command.
Designed the platform to be extensible beyond frontend apps too — Lambda-based services could plug into the same shared pipeline instead of needing their own bespoke setup.
sections.eli5: Think of it like ordering a food truck. Launching a brand-new frontend app used to mean building your own truck from scratch — get a vehicle, wire the kitchen, sort the permits — all before serving a single dish. We built a system where one order gets you a fully licensed, wired, ready-to-park truck, so you go straight to cooking: writing the actual app, instead of the plumbing around it.
sections.heading: Web Applications Platform (WAP)

bullets: ExpressVPN grew quickly, with hiring waves and periods of headcount reduction along the way — and onboarding/offboarding was entirely manual: HR cloned a Google Sheet checklist and worked through it by hand, application by application, for every employee.

Built a SCIM connector for Okta to automate provisioning and deprovisioning — including writing connectors from scratch for apps that didn't support SCIM out of the box, and for internal, in-house-built applications too, so offboarding wasn't limited to off-the-shelf SaaS tools.
Applied the same monorepo pattern built for WAP to house the SCIM connectors — one shared platform instead of a one-off integration per app.
Also built integrations with Airtable, which management relied on heavily day to day — meeting the org where its actual tools were rather than pushing everyone onto a "correct" one.
sections.eli5: Think of offboarding like flipping light switches in a large building — before, HR walked room to room, manually flipping every switch (revoking access to every application) off a paper checklist. We wired a master switch instead: flip it once and every room's access shuts off automatically, including custom-built rooms that didn't come with a standard switch, where one got wired in ourselves. And instead of wiring each room differently, every switch lived in the same shared control panel — the same pattern already built for WAP.
sections.heading: Internal Apps & Automation (IAA)

bullets: Standardized local development with devcontainers and golden Docker images — particularly valuable for legacy systems that were previously painful to set up by hand. Beyond faster onboarding, this made it easy for engineers to move across teams and jump in to help, which mattered in a company that reorganized often.

Modernized the cloud setup with IaC modules on Scalr, replacing what had been a "wild west" of teams running their own AWS accounts however they liked. This enforced consistent resource tagging, so cloud cost could finally be attributed accurately to the team responsible for it.

Standardized on ECS as the default compute platform, reserving Kubernetes for cases with a genuinely strong justification — making cost and maintenance predictable, and cutting out a recurring source of tech-stack debate between teams.
sections.eli5: Think of it like running an apartment building. Devcontainers meant every unit came fully furnished and move-in ready — including the older, oddly-wired units that used to take days to set up — so any tenant (engineer) could move between units (teams) without reassembling furniture each time. On the finance side, tenants used to run their own separate accounts and spend however they liked, a real wild west. We put everyone on one shared, metered account instead, so costs traced back to the right tenant, and set a standard unit layout (ECS) that covers almost every need, reserving custom-built layouts (Kubernetes) for the rare case that actually needs one — which also ended a lot of arguments about whose layout was best.
sections.heading: Platform Team

bullets: Consolidated the subscription and payment systems of multiple VPN brands (including PIA and CyberGhost) owned by ExpressVPN's parent company into a single unified platform.

The hardest technical part was correctness during the migration itself — the platform couldn't afford downtime, so relied on Change Data Capture (CDC) to keep the old and new systems in sync in real time throughout the cutover, rather than a big-bang switch.

The harder part wasn't technical at all: a change in leadership late in the project brought real hesitation about whether to proceed, out of concern for how consolidation might affect one brand's distinct market position. Helping build the confidence to see the migration through to completion mattered as much as getting the migration itself right.
Collaborated with the marketing team on targeted email campaigns offering discounts to customers at risk of cancelling, helping win back lapsed subscribers.
sections.eli5: Imagine several sibling stores (different VPN brands) each running their own separate cash register — this project merged them into one shared register, so a pricing change or subscription update applies everywhere at once instead of being repeated four times. The tricky part was making the swap without ever closing the doors — customers kept shopping while the register got rewired underneath them — and, near the finish line, convincing store management that sharing a register wouldn't make their flagship store look like just another branch.

experiences.title: Summer Intern - Cybersecurity Agency of Singapore (CSA)

bullets: Reviewed open-source code libraries used in sensitive government projects to identify potential security weaknesses before they could be exploited.
This is where I first learned to use static analysis tools like SonarQube — a habit that's stuck ever since; it's one of the first things I set up on any team I join now.
Also picked up a skill that mattered more than expected at the time: quickly telling real vulnerabilities apart from the false positives these tools throw off constantly.

Alongside the audit work, built a small side project with another intern — an Android app that detects whether you've actually lost internet access, not just Wi-Fi, by pinging an outside server rather than just checking if you're connected to a router.
On my last day, my supervisor gave me a book — Winning with Honour — a small gesture that's stuck with me longer than most of the technical work did.
sections.eli5: Being connected to Wi-Fi doesn't mean you have working internet — it's like being plugged into a phone line where the call never actually connects. The app didn't just check whether the phone was plugged in; it checked whether the call went through.
